questions.stem: After the 1900 handoff on a cardiac step-down unit, the nurse reviews four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client with chronic atrial fibrillation whose heart rate is 88/min and irregular and who is due a scheduled dose of apixaban
A client with new atrial fibrillation at 152/min who says they feel dizzy and whose blood pressure has dropped to 86/50 mm Hg
A client 2 days after a pacemaker insertion who asks for help walking to the bathroom and has a small, dry dressing over the pocket
A client with heart failure who gained 0.5 kg (1.1 lb) since yesterday and has mild ankle swelling that is unchanged from admission

rationale.correct: An unstable rhythm with hypotension and symptoms comes before stable chronic conditions and routine needs.

perOption.a: Controlled chronic atrial fibrillation is expected; the dose can be given after the unstable client is seen.
perOption.b: A rapid ventricular rate with dizziness and hypotension shows poor cardiac output and possible instability.
perOption.c: This client is stable; the request can be met by assistive personnel or after the priority client.
perOption.d: A small weight change with unchanged edema is not urgent.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize a client with an unstable rhythm.

questions.stem: On a pediatric unit, the RN is working with an assistive personnel (AP). Which task should the RN delegate to the AP?

options.text: Weighing a 6-month-old infant with gastroenteritis on the same scale before the morning feeding
Watching a 4-year-old with croup for retractions and stridor after a dose of racemic epinephrine
Feeding a 2-month-old with a cleft palate for the first time with a special bottle and nipple
Teaching the parent of a 7-year-old with new type 1 diabetes how to draw up and give insulin

rationale.correct: Delegate routine, predictable tasks for stable clients; keep assessment after treatment, first-time complex care and teaching.

perOption.a: Weighing a stable infant is a routine task with set steps that AP are trained to do; the RN interprets the result.
perOption.b: Observing for rebound airway narrowing after treatment needs RN assessment.
perOption.c: The first feeding with special equipment needs the RN's skill and judgment to watch for aspiration.
perOption.d: Teaching is the RN's responsibility and cannot be delegated to AP.

questions.stem: The RN on a busy medical unit is working with a licensed practical nurse (LPN). Which 2 tasks are appropriate for the RN to give to the LPN?

options.text: Giving scheduled oral medications to a stable client with diabetes and hypertension
Completing the admission assessment of a client just arrived from the emergency department with chest pain
Changing a dry sterile dressing on a client with a healing abdominal incision
Developing the discharge teaching plan for a client starting home peritoneal dialysis
Evaluating whether a client's pain has improved 30 minutes after a first dose of IV morphine

rationale.correct: LPNs give medications and treatments to stable clients; RNs keep initial assessment, care planning, initial teaching and evaluation of new therapies.

perOption.a: Oral medications for stable clients are within LPN scope.
perOption.b: The initial assessment of a new, possibly unstable client is the RN's responsibility.
perOption.c: Dressing changes on stable wounds are within LPN scope.
perOption.d: Planning and initial teaching are RN responsibilities.
perOption.e: Evaluating the response to a new IV opioid needs RN judgment.

questions.stem: A nurse who has just finished orientation on a medical unit is floated to the intensive care unit. The ICU charge nurse is making the assignment. Which assignment is most appropriate for this nurse?

options.text: A client on a ventilator who is receiving a titrated norepinephrine infusion
A client with an intracranial pressure monitor and an external ventricular drain
A stable client awaiting transfer to a medical unit who needs routine care and medications
A client who arrived 30 minutes ago in diabetic ketoacidosis with an insulin drip being started

rationale.correct: Float nurses receive the most stable clients whose care matches their training, with an experienced resource nurse available.

perOption.a: Titrating vasopressors for a ventilated client needs ICU-level skills.
perOption.b: ICP monitoring and drains are specialized ICU care.
perOption.c: A float nurse should receive a stable client whose needs match their experience.
perOption.d: A new, unstable admission on an insulin infusion needs an experienced ICU nurse.

questions.stem: A client who signed the consent for a knee arthroscopy yesterday says, while being moved to the operating room, "I've changed my mind. I don't want the surgery." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remind the client that the consent form was signed yesterday, so the surgery will go ahead as planned
Stop the transfer and notify the surgeon that the client has withdrawn consent
Give the prescribed preoperative sedative to calm the client's nerves before surgery
Ask the client's family to talk the client into having the surgery today as planned

rationale.correct: Consent can be withdrawn at any time before the procedure; stop, notify the surgeon and document.

perOption.a: Consent can be withdrawn at any time, even after signing.
perOption.b: A competent client may withdraw consent at any point; the surgeon must be told before anything else happens.
perOption.c: Sedating a client who has withdrawn consent would be battery.
perOption.d: Pressuring the client undermines a voluntary decision.

questions.stem: On admission, a client with advanced COPD says, "I have a living will at home that says I don't want to be put on a breathing machine." No copy is in the record. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client the living will does not count unless it is signed again at the hospital
Ask the family to bring a copy, document the client's stated wishes and tell the provider
Write a do-not-intubate order in the record based on what the client has told the nurse
Wait until the client becomes too ill to speak, then call the family to ask about the document

rationale.correct: Ask about advance directives on admission, place copies in the record and inform the provider, who discusses and writes code status orders.

perOption.a: A valid living will made earlier still applies; a new one is not required.
perOption.b: Getting the document into the record and telling the provider makes sure the client's wishes guide care.
perOption.c: Nurses do not write code status orders; the provider writes them after discussion with the client.
perOption.d: Waiting risks care that goes against the client's wishes.

questions.educationalObjective: Act on a client's advance directive.

questions.stem: A police officer comes to the emergency department and asks the nurse for the blood alcohol result of a client involved in a car crash. The client has not given permission. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the result, since police investigations are an exception to privacy rules
Explain it needs the client's consent or legal authority, and refer the request
Show the officer the result on the computer screen without printing or copying it
Ask the client's spouse whether the nurse can give the result to the officer who is waiting

rationale.correct: Release health information to police only with the client's consent or a valid legal requirement; refer such requests to the supervisor or privacy officer.

perOption.a: Disclosure to police generally needs the client's permission, a court order, a warrant or another legal requirement.
perOption.b: The nurse protects the information and refers the request to the supervisor or privacy officer to decide whether a legal exception applies.
perOption.c: Showing the screen is still a disclosure.
perOption.d: The spouse cannot authorize disclosure for a competent adult.

questions.stem: A medical-surgical nurse is floated to the cardiac unit and is assigned a client who needs a titrated amiodarone and nitroglycerin infusion. The nurse has never titrated these drugs. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Refuse the whole assignment and go back to the home unit until a better fit is available
Tell the charge nurse and ask for a different client or for help with the infusions
Accept the assignment and look up the titration protocols online during the shift
Accept the assignment and ask the client's family to report any changes in the client's symptoms

rationale.correct: Accept the parts of an assignment you can perform safely, tell the charge nurse about any gaps in competence, and ask for a change or supervision.

perOption.a: Refusing the whole assignment can be abandonment; the nurse should accept what they can do safely and ask for help with the rest.
perOption.b: Nurses must practice within their competence; telling the charge nurse lets the assignment be changed or support be provided.
perOption.c: Learning a high-alert skill alone during care is unsafe.
perOption.d: Families cannot monitor high-alert infusions.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to an assignment outside one's competence.

questions.stem: The nurse realizes they wrote a client's blood pressure in the wrong client's paper flowsheet. How should the nurse correct the entry?

options.text: Draw one line through it, write "mistaken entry" and add the date, time and initials
Cover the wrong entry with correction fluid and write the right value neatly on top
Scribble over the entry until it cannot be read, then continue below it
Tear out the page and copy the other correct entries onto a new, clean flowsheet page

rationale.correct: Correct paper records with a single line, a note of the error, the date, time and initials; never erase, obscure or remove entries.

perOption.a: A single line keeps the original readable and shows who corrected it and when.
perOption.b: Correction fluid hides the original and looks like tampering.
perOption.c: Obliterating entries is not acceptable in a legal record.
perOption.d: Removing pages from the record is falsification.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: While preparing medications, the nurse notices that the automated dispensing cabinet released hydromorphone 2 mg tablets when the prescription is for 0.5 mg. The nurse catches the error before giving anything. What should the nurse do after getting the correct dose?

options.text: Do nothing more, since the client was not harmed and no error reached them
Report the near miss through the facility's safety reporting system
Write a note in the client's record that the wrong strength was dispensed
Tell the pharmacy technician privately so they can be more careful next time

rationale.correct: Near misses are reported through the safety system so system causes can be found and fixed; they are not charted in the client's record.

perOption.a: Near misses reveal system weaknesses and should be reported so they can be fixed.
perOption.b: Reporting near misses lets the facility find and fix problems such as a cabinet stocking error before someone is harmed.
perOption.c: Event details go in the safety report, not the client's record.
perOption.d: Informal feedback alone does not allow the system to be analyzed and fixed.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client is ready for discharge 4 days after hip fracture surgery. The client needs help with transfers and walking, lives alone in a second-floor apartment and wants to return home eventually. Which discharge setting should the case manager most likely recommend?

options.text: Home today with a list of exercises to do alone each day
Short-term rehabilitation in a skilled nursing or rehab facility
Permanent placement in a long-term care facility, since the client is 84
Home with a family member visiting once a week to check on the client and bring groceries

rationale.correct: Discharge settings match the client's functional needs and goals; short-term rehabilitation bridges the gap when home is not yet safe.

perOption.a: The client cannot transfer or walk safely alone and lives up a flight of stairs.
perOption.b: Short-term rehabilitation provides daily therapy and nursing until the client can safely return home.
perOption.c: Age alone does not mean permanent placement; the client's goal is to return home.
perOption.d: Weekly visits do not meet the client's daily need for help with transfers.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A client with a new permanent tracheostomy after laryngeal cancer surgery is being discharged to live with their spouse. Which referral is most important for a safe transition home?

options.text: A dietitian, to plan high-calorie meals that the client can swallow easily
Home health nursing and a home medical equipment supplier for suction and humidification
A social worker, to help the client apply for disability benefits after discharge
A support group for people who have had cancer surgery of the head or neck, to help with coping

rationale.correct: For a new tracheostomy, arrange home health nursing and equipment (suction, humidification, supplies) before discharge.

perOption.a: Nutrition matters, but airway care at home is the main safety need.
perOption.b: The client and spouse need follow-up for tracheostomy care and the equipment to keep the airway clear at home.
perOption.c: Financial support may be needed, but airway safety comes first.
perOption.d: Support groups help coping, but the most important need is safe airway management.

questions.stem: The nurse finds a client sitting on the floor beside the bed. Place the nurse's actions in order.

items.text: Call for help and stay with the client
Help the client back to bed safely with enough staff or a lift
Notify the provider and the family, and complete an incident report
Assess the client for injury, including head injury, before moving them

rationale.correct: After a fall: call for help, assess before moving, move safely, then notify and report.

perOption.a: The nurse gets help without leaving the client alone.
perOption.b: Moving an injured client can worsen harm.
perOption.c: The client is moved only after injury is ruled out.
perOption.d: Notification and reporting follow care.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a client fall in order.

questions.stem: A client being discharged asks the nurse to email their lab results and discharge papers to their personal email address. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Email the documents from the nurse's own email so the client gets them quickly
Show the client how to view the results in the secure patient portal and give printed papers
Text photos of the documents to the client's phone using the nurse's own mobile phone
Tell the client that results are given out in person at a follow-up clinic visit

rationale.correct: Share health information through secure channels such as patient portals or printed copies, not personal email or texts.

perOption.a: Personal email is not secure and breaches privacy policies.
perOption.b: Patient portals and printed copies share information securely according to policy.
perOption.c: Photos on personal devices are not secure.
perOption.d: Clients have the right to their results, and secure electronic access is available.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: At 0630, two RNs call in sick for the day shift on a 30-bed medical unit, leaving three RNs and two AP. What should the charge nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the night nurses to stay for the whole day shift without asking whether they are able to
Notify the staffing office or supervisor to request additional staff and review client acuity
Close the unit to new admissions without telling the house supervisor about the decision
Give each RN ten clients and tell the two AP to complete the morning assessments

rationale.correct: When staffing is short, escalate early to the supervisor or staffing office, assign by acuity and delegate within scope.

perOption.a: Mandating exhausted staff for a full shift is unsafe; any overtime should be voluntary and short.
perOption.b: The charge nurse escalates the shortage early and uses acuity to plan assignments while help is found.
perOption.c: Diverting admissions is a system-level decision made through the supervisor.
perOption.d: AP cannot do assessments, and unsafe loads should be escalated, not accepted.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse with strong personal beliefs against elective abortion works in a hospital where these procedures are scheduled on the gynecology unit. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse?

options.text: Refuse to care for any client on the unit who has had or plans an abortion
Tell the nurse manager about the objection in advance so assignments can be planned
Accept the assignment but avoid speaking with the client during the shift
Share personal views with clients so that they can choose another nurse if they would like to

rationale.correct: Nurses may decline to take part in some procedures on moral grounds by telling their employer in advance, but they must not abandon clients or refuse emergency care.

perOption.a: Nurses cannot refuse basic or emergency care to clients because of personal beliefs.
perOption.b: Conscientious objection is raised in advance through the facility's process so care is not disrupted and clients are not abandoned.
perOption.c: Withholding communication harms care and the client's dignity.
perOption.d: Sharing personal views with clients is unprofessional and may pressure them.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client who is alert, oriented and able to make decisions wants to go home after a stroke rehabilitation stay. The client's adult children insist on a nursing home and ask the nurse to "make sure it happens." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client that the family has decided a nursing home is safest
Support the client's decision and arrange a team meeting to plan a safe discharge home
Ask the provider to declare the client unable to make decisions so the family can decide
Avoid getting involved, since this is a disagreement within the family to settle alone

rationale.correct: A client with decision-making capacity has the right to choose where to live; the nurse advocates and helps plan a safe discharge.

perOption.a: A competent client makes their own decisions about where to live.
perOption.b: The nurse advocates for the client's choice and involves the team in planning services to make home safe.
perOption.c: Capacity is determined by assessment, not to settle a family disagreement.
perOption.d: The nurse has a duty to advocate for the client.

questions.educationalObjective: Advocate for a competent older adult's choice.

questions.stem: At 1100 an assistive personnel (AP) gives the nurse this report. Highlight the findings that need the nurse's follow-up.

segments.text: Room 6 says their chest feels "heavy" since walking to the bathroom
walked twice in the hall with a walker
had a bath and a linen change
Room 12 has had no urine in the catheter bag since 0700

rationale.correct: The RN follows up on reported data that suggest a change in condition, such as chest symptoms, fever or no urine output.

perOption.s2: New chest heaviness after exertion may be cardiac and needs RN assessment now.
perOption.s6: A new fever needs assessment and reporting.
perOption.s10: No urine output for 4 hours suggests a blocked catheter or a kidney problem.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize reported findings that need follow-up.

questions.stem: The nurse receives four telephone calls from clients of an outpatient surgery center. For each caller, indicate how urgently the nurse should act.

rows.text: Two days after a tonsillectomy, spitting out bright red blood several times in the last hour
One day after a hernia repair, mild incision pain controlled with acetaminophen and asks about showering
Three days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, temperature 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) and redness at one port site
One day after a knee arthroscopy, sudden shortness of breath and chest pain

columns.text: Send to the emergency department now

rationale.correct: Telephone triage: life-threatening signs go to emergency care now; possible complications need same-day follow-up; simple questions get routine advice.

perOption.r1:c1: Active bleeding after tonsillectomy can be life-threatening.
perOption.r1:c2: Waiting is unsafe with active bleeding.
perOption.r1:c3: This is not a routine question.
perOption.r3:c1: No signs of sepsis or emergency are described.
perOption.r3:c2: Possible wound infection needs advice and same-day follow-up.
perOption.r3:c3: Fever and redness need more than routine advice.
perOption.r4:c1: These symptoms after surgery can mean a pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: In January, a parent calls the clinic saying everyone in the family has had headaches, nausea and dizziness for 2 days that get better when they are away from home. The house uses a gas furnace. What should the nurse tell the parent first?

options.text: Give everyone acetaminophen and plenty of fluids, then call back if they are not better tomorrow
Get everyone out of the house into fresh air now and call emergency services
Open the windows tonight and schedule a furnace inspection for later this week
Bring the whole family to the clinic tomorrow morning for flu tests and an exam

rationale.correct: Suspect carbon monoxide when household members share headache, nausea and dizziness that improve away from home; leave the building and call emergency services.

perOption.a: These symptoms in the whole family suggest carbon monoxide poisoning, which can be fatal.
perOption.b: Symptoms that ease away from home in a household with a gas furnace suggest carbon monoxide; leaving and calling for help is the first step.
perOption.c: Staying in the home risks more exposure; the family must leave now.
perOption.d: Delay can be fatal if this is carbon monoxide poisoning.

questions.stem: In which situation should the nurse wear clean gloves?

options.text: Taking a client's blood pressure on intact skin
Emptying a urinary catheter drainage bag
Helping a client put on their slippers before walking
Handing a client a cup of water and their menu

rationale.correct: Standard precautions: gloves when touching blood, body fluids, mucous membranes or broken skin, with hand hygiene before and after.

perOption.a: Gloves are not needed for contact with intact skin.
perOption.b: Standard precautions require gloves when contact with body fluids is expected.
perOption.c: Gloves are not needed for this contact.
perOption.d: Gloves are not needed for this contact.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply standard precautions for glove use.

questions.stem: A newly hired nurse with no risk factors other than working in a hospital has a tuberculin skin test read 48 hours after placement. The induration measures 12 mm. How should the nurse interpret the result?

options.text: Negative, because induration of 15 mm or more is needed to call it positive in health care workers
Positive, and the nurse needs a chest x-ray and evaluation for tuberculosis
Positive for active tuberculosis, so the nurse stops working today and begins four-drug treatment
Inconclusive, because the test has to be read at exactly 24 hours to be valid

rationale.correct: TST cut-offs: 5 mm for high-risk groups such as HIV or close contacts, 10 mm for health care workers and other moderate-risk groups, 15 mm for people with no risk factors.

perOption.a: 15 mm is the cut-off for people with no risk factors; health care workers use 10 mm.
perOption.b: For health care workers, 10 mm or more is positive; a chest x-ray and assessment for active disease follow.
perOption.c: A positive skin test shows infection, not necessarily active disease; evaluation comes first.
perOption.d: TST is read at 48 to 72 hours.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give an IV chemotherapy drug. Which precautions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves
Wear a disposable, low-permeability gown that closes in the back
Prime the IV tubing at the bedside by letting the drug drip into the trash
Dispose of used equipment in a labeled hazardous drug container
Wear a surgical mask only when the client is coughing

rationale.correct: Hazardous drug safety: double chemotherapy gloves, protective gown, closed-system devices where possible, no bedside priming with the drug and hazardous waste disposal.

perOption.a: Double gloving reduces skin exposure.
perOption.b: A protective gown prevents the drug from reaching clothing and skin.
perOption.c: Tubing is primed with a non-drug solution or in the pharmacy to avoid releasing the drug.
perOption.d: Hazardous waste goes in designated containers.
perOption.e: A mask does not address the main exposure routes, and respiratory protection is used only if aerosolization is possible.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client on an inpatient psychiatric unit has been placed in seclusion after assaulting a staff member. Which action by the nurse meets safety standards for seclusion?

options.text: Checking on the client through the window once an hour and charting the findings
Keeping the client under continuous observation and offering fluids and toileting regularly
Leaving the client in seclusion until the next morning's team meeting decides the next step
Using seclusion because the unit is short-staffed and the client needs a lot of attention

rationale.correct: Seclusion is a last resort for imminent danger: it needs an order, continuous observation, care of basic needs and release as soon as safe.

perOption.a: Clients in seclusion need continuous observation, not hourly checks.
perOption.b: Seclusion requires continuous monitoring and attention to basic needs, with release as soon as it is safe.
perOption.c: Seclusion ends as soon as the client is no longer a danger, and orders must be renewed within set time limits.
perOption.d: Seclusion cannot be used for staff convenience or as punishment.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A fire on the floor below forces the evacuation of a medical unit. In what order should the nurse move clients?

options.text: Clients on ventilators first, because they are the sickest and need the most help
Ambulatory clients first, then clients in wheelchairs, then bedbound clients
Bedbound clients first, then wheelchair users, then clients who can walk
Clients in the rooms nearest the stairs first, whatever their mobility

rationale.correct: Horizontal or vertical evacuation usually moves ambulatory clients first, then wheelchair users, then bedbound clients, unless one area is in immediate danger.

perOption.a: Moving the most dependent first delays the largest number of people who could leave quickly.
perOption.b: Moving those who can walk first gets the most people out fastest, and frees staff for clients who need more help.
perOption.c: This order uses many staff for few clients early and delays the others.
perOption.d: Room location alone does not get the most people out safely.
